issues.legal_issue: An agreement for sale is concluded when the seller accepts earnest money and gives a receipt recording the agreed sale, despite later disputes about preparation of the conveyance.
material_facts: The seller accepted earnest money and issued a signed receipt stating that it was paid toward the agreed sale of the property for a specified total price and that a sale deed would be executed within three months.
The receipt and acceptance of the money were admitted.
The defences that the agreement was induced by fraud or misrepresentation did not displace the receipt as evidence of the concluded agreement.
issues.conclusion: The parties made a completed and binding contract for sale, which the purchaser was entitled to have specifically performed.
issues.legal_principle: The purchaser bore the initial burden of proving the contract. The seller’s admitted receipt, recording earnest money toward the sale, supported the finding of a concluded contract and shifted the evidentiary burden to those seeking to explain it away. The court also considered the pleadings and the absence of a clear, supported case that no final agreement had been made.

predicates.purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance: A purchaser sued to compel performance of an alleged contract for sale.
predicates.seller_accepted_earnest_and_issued_contr: The seller accepted earnest money and issued a receipt recording that it was paid toward the agreed sale.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks specific performance and the seller accepted earnest money and issued a receipt recording the agreed sale, the sale contract is concluded.

issues.legal_issue: A later disagreement about the form of a title warranty in the conveyance does not undo a concluded sale contract or amount to repudiation when the purchaser does not persist in the demand and remains ready to perform the agreed contract.
material_facts: After the sale contract had been made, the purchaser’s broker presented a draft conveyance containing a particular form of title warranty to which the seller’s manager objected.
The evidence and pleadings did not show that the purchaser refused to complete the sale unless that particular warranty was included.
The purchaser later called for completion of the conveyance as agreed and expressed readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
issues.conclusion: The later dispute over the warranty neither affected the completeness of the earlier contract nor amounted to repudiation.
issues.legal_principle: A post-contract proposal about the form of a conveyance must be distinguished from a refusal to perform the contract. A demand for a warranty to which a party is not entitled may, in appropriate circumstances, disentitle that party to specific performance, as considered in Bindeshri Prasad v. Mahant Jairam Gir, I.L.R. 9 All. 705; but a proposal not persisted in, alongside readiness to perform the agreed contract, is not repudiation.

rule.if: purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance and warranty_dispute_arose_after_contract and purchaser_did_not_persist_in_warranty_demand and purchaser_remained_ready_to_perform

predicates.purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance: A purchaser sued to compel performance of an alleged contract for sale.
predicates.warranty_dispute_arose_after_contract: The parties disputed the form of a warranty while preparing the conveyance after making the sale contract.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_persist_in_warranty_de: The purchaser did not maintain that the sale would be completed only if the disputed form of warranty were included.
predicates.purchaser_remained_ready_to_perform: The purchaser called for completion on the agreed terms and remained ready and willing to perform.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, a later warranty dispute does not undo the contract or amount to repudiation if the purchaser does not persist in the demand and remains ready to perform.

issues.legal_issue: When specific performance is sought against a seller and a subsequent transferee whose title has passed to them, the decree should require the seller to perform the original contract and the transferee to join the conveyance to pass that title to the purchaser.
material_facts: The seller had made an earlier contract to sell the property to the plaintiff and subsequently conveyed the property to the appealing purchasers.
The court concluded that the earlier contract was binding and entitled the plaintiff to specific performance.
The title resided in the subsequent transferees, while the original contract’s terms and covenants were between the seller and the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The seller was to execute a sale deed in accordance with the original contract, and the subsequent transferees were to join the conveyance solely to pass their title to the plaintiff.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 91 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, 3 illustration (g) and 27 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and 40 of the Transfer of Property Act address the subsequent transferee’s obligation and when it may be enforced, but do not directly prescribe the form of decree. The decree should avoid cancelling the later transfer, which may disturb equities between its parties, and should not force the transferee to assume covenants from a contract to which they were not a party. The court followed Kafiladdin v. Samiraddin, A.I.R. 1931 Cal. 67, and the English practice reflected in Potter v. Sanders, 67 E.R. 1057, and declined the approach in Kali Charan v. Janak Deo, A.I.R. 1932 All. 694, which involved cancellation of the later sale.

predicates.purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance: A purchaser sued to compel performance of an earlier contract for sale.
predicates.later_transferee_holds_title_under_subse: A subsequent transferee holds title to the property under a later transfer from the seller.

issues.definition: Where a purchaser seeks specific performance and a later transferee holds title under a subsequent transfer, the seller performs the original contract and the transferee joins only to pass title.

issues.legal_issue: The balance of the purchase price is not automatically payable to a subsequent transferee, but the court may direct payment from money deposited for specific performance when the circumstances and established equities justify that relief.
material_facts: The plaintiff had deposited the full unpaid purchase price in court as a condition of obtaining the conveyance.
The subsequent transferees claimed to have paid consideration for their purchase and were willing to settle on terms under which they would be compensated from the deposit.

The seller was outside the jurisdiction, and the Custodian representing the seller’s estate opposed the proposed settlement but could not identify any term of the contract or conveyance that barred the subsequent transferees from recovering their consideration from the seller.
The court found it inequitable to leave the subsequent transferees to pursue potentially fruitless litigation while the seller’s estate retained the deposited money.
issues.conclusion: In the circumstances, the subsequent transferees were to receive compensation from the deposit, with the balance available to the Custodian after the conveyance was completed.
issues.legal_principle: There is no general rule that the balance of the purchase price must be paid to a subsequent transferee up to the amount that transferee paid. Equities between the seller and transferee may make that improper, so those equities should ordinarily be raised and decided. In this case the court exercised its equitable discretion because the money remained in court, the seller was beyond its jurisdiction, and no basis had been shown to defeat the transferees’ claim against the seller’s estate.

rule.if: purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance and purchase_money_deposited_in_court and subsequent_transferee_paid_consideration and vendor_cannot_be_reached_for_effective_recovery and no_equity_bar_to_transferee_recovery_is_shown

predicates.purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance: A purchaser sued to compel performance of an earlier contract for sale.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited_in_court: The purchase money was deposited in court in connection with the decree for specific performance.
predicates.subsequent_transferee_paid_consideration: A subsequent transferee paid consideration to acquire the property.
predicates.vendor_cannot_be_reached_for_effective_r: The vendor was beyond the court’s jurisdiction, making effective recovery from the vendor uncertain or impracticable.
predicates.no_equity_bar_to_transferee_recovery_is_: No relevant contractual term, covenant, or other established equity was shown to prevent the transferee from recovering from the vendor.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks specific performance, purchase money is deposited in court, a subsequent transferee paid for the property, effective recovery from the vendor is impracticable, and no bar to the transferee’s recovery is shown, the court may allocate the deposit to compensate the transferee.
